strengths: Strong theoretical framework: Theorem 4.1 proves global optimality of greedy polynomial selection through elegant application of approximation theory and equioscillation theorem
GPU-optimized design: Uses only matrix-matrix products (no QR/inverses), enabling half-precision (bfloat16) execution with careful finite-precision handling
Well-written and comprehensive: Clear exposition with detailed proofs, concrete algorithms with code, and thoughtful treatment of numerical stability issues
Thorough experimental validation: Includes synthetic matrices, real GPT-2 gradients, and full training runs across learning rates with consistent improvements
Practical relevance: Directly applicable to increasingly popular Muon optimizer for large-scale LLM training
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Builds incrementally on Chen & Chow (2014) rescaling strategy; for degree-3, Polar Express is essentially equivalent; main contribution is generalizing to degree-5 and proving optimality
Modest empirical improvements: ~1.6% relative loss improvement (3.340 vs 3.400) without statistical significance testing or error bars; practical impact unclear
Loose theoretical analysis: Theorem 4.3 acknowledged to underestimate convergence rate ('about twice as fast'); gap between theory and practice suggests framework incompleteness
Lower bound sensitivity: The guessed parameter ℓ significantly affects convergence (Figure 4 shows 2-order-magnitude error delays convergence); undermines optimality claims when ℓ is unknown
Limited experimental scope: Only GPT-2 models (124M, 774M) on FineWeb dataset; missing experiments on larger models, different datasets/architectures, or beyond-Muon applications
Incomplete baselines: QDWH mentioned but not experimentally compared; You's method only defined for 6 iterations; missing comparison with concurrent Grishina et al. (2025) work
Missing ablations: No systematic study of polynomial degree d or iteration count T; limited analysis of finite-precision modifications' impact; spectrum-aware initialization not integrated
Reproducibility gaps: No random seeds, error bars, or multiple runs reported; limited training details; only H100 GPU tested

Limited mechanistic insight: Improvements largest in early iterations where all methods already converge well; insufficient analysis of which matrix properties favor Polar Express or why adaptivity helps

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem of computing polar decompositions efficiently on GPUs in low precision
Sound mathematical framework with correct application of equioscillation theory (Theorem 4.1 and Lemma A.1)
Clear presentation with simple, reproducible Algorithm 1 implementation
Thorough engineering details for practical bfloat16 arithmetic (Section 4.4)
Reasonable experimental scope including synthetic matrices, real gradient matrices, and end-to-end GPT-2 training
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily adapts Zolo-pd (Nakatsukasa & Freund, 2016) and Chen & Chow (2014) to polynomials; concurrent work [19] does essentially the same thing
Theorem 4.1 follows relatively straightforwardly from classical Equioscillation Theorem via induction; greedy approach is natural rather than surprising
Modest empirical improvements (1-2% validation loss reduction) that lack statistical significance testing or error bars
Unfair experimental comparisons: different methods trained with different learning rates (Figure 1 shows 0.02 for Muon variants vs 0.0001 for AdamW)
Practical limitations inadequately addressed: method requires bounds [ℓ, u] on singular values; Figure 4 shows two orders of magnitude error significantly degrades performance
Ad-hoc finite-precision modifications (safety factor 1.01, cushioning at u/10, normalization offset 10^-2) lack principled justification and break theoretical optimality guarantees
Limited experimental scope: single dataset (FineWeb), models only up to 774M parameters (while Muon has been used on 32B models), single seed/epoch
No wall-clock time comparisons in most figures; Algorithm 4 for rectangular matrices (Appendix F) shows no practical benefit despite 5 pages of development
Critical algorithmic details relegated to appendices; unclear how polynomial coefficients are computed for new settings
Missing ablation studies on degree d, number of iterations T, and individual finite-precision modifications

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.1 elegantly proves that greedy composition of minimax-optimal polynomials is globally optimal, connecting approximation theory to iterative methods in a novel way
Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates why polynomial methods are necessary for GPU-friendly deep learning (avoiding inverses/QR decompositions) versus classical numerical methods

Comprehensive practical contribution: Includes closed-form solutions for degree-3, Remez-like algorithm for degree-5, finite-precision handling, clean implementation (Algorithm 1), and offline/online split
Solid experimental validation: Tests on synthetic matrices, real GPT-2 gradients, and large-scale training (1B tokens) with consistent improvements across learning rates
Clear, implementable presentation: Practical algorithms are concrete and compilable; paper balances rigor with practicality through strategic use of appendices
Consistent empirical improvements: Validation loss improvements of 0.04-0.06 points maintained across different model scales and hyperparameter settings
Timely application: Addresses efficiency needs of increasingly popular Muon optimizer for LLM training
weaknesses: Modest practical improvements: Validation loss gains (~0.06 points) are consistent but not transformative; Appendix F.1 shows negligible speedup from Algorithm 4 at current scales
Theoretical-practical gap: Theorem 4.1 proves optimality for computing polar(M), but no analysis of how this improves Muon's convergence rates; connection remains empirical
Singular value bound dependency: Method requires choosing lower bound ℓ; choice of 10^{-3} for bfloat16 appears empirically driven; Figure 4 shows sensitivity to ℓ on real matrices
Ad-hoc finite-precision fixes: Safety factors (1.01), cushioning thresholds (0.024), and non-monotonicity handling lack theoretical justification; acknowledged as 'somewhat arbitrary'
Limited experimental scope: Only GPT-2 tested (124M-774M params), single dataset (FineWeb), no other architectures; unclear if benefits scale to 7B+ models or different settings

Unclear novelty boundaries: Chen & Chow [12] already proposed adaptive methods for degree-3; Zolo-pd [38] uses similar interval-based adaptation; concurrent work [19] proposes nearly identical approach
Missing practical comparisons: No equal-FLOP Newton-Schulz baseline; no end-to-end training time comparisons; Figure 5 shows degree-3 Chen & Chow is competitive

Unused appendix material: Appendices E-F propose interesting ideas (spectrum-aware initialization, rectangular acceleration) but Appendix F.1 explicitly states these provide 'negligible benefits' at current scales, adding length without supporting main claims
Reproducibility concerns: FineWeb access may be limited; some hyperparameter choices appear data-specific; the 0.024 cushioning factor seems oddly specific

strengths: Clean theoretical result (Theorem 3.1) proving optimality of greedy polynomial composition with elegant proof using Equioscillation Theorem
Well-motivated GPU-friendly algorithm design with only matrix-matrix products, practical for bfloat16 arithmetic
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with proper ablations, multiple datasets/scales, and reproducible code
Consistent improvements across learning rates and training settings (1B-10B tokens), though modest in magnitude
Practical algorithm already adopted in NanoGPT; clear implementation (30 lines of PyTorch)
Strong attention to finite-precision considerations and reproducibility with full proofs/code in appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: greedy polynomial selection from Chen & Chow (2014); Remez algorithm classical; main contribution is extending to d=5 and proving global optimality

Significant theory-practice gap: worst-case minimax formulation assumes all singular values equally important, but Figure 9 shows Muon insensitive to singular values <10⁻³σ_max; this fundamental mismatch not adequately addressed
Modest empirical improvements: GPT-2-Large 1.7% improvement, GPT-2-Small 1.1%; no advantage on image classification; improvements shrink at 10B tokens

Experimental limitation: all methods use identical computational cost (5 iterations of degree-5 polynomials), so improvement is purely approximation quality within fixed budget; polar computation not the bottleneck
Incomplete evaluation: largest model 774M parameters; no experiments on modern scales (billion+); claims about 1T parameter models lack validation
Brittle parameter choices: lower bound ℓ=10⁻³ is a 'guess'; Figure 3 shows high sensitivity to ℓ; safety factors/cushioning in Section G are ad-hoc workarounds for numerical instability
Disconnected contributions: Sections I and J feel tangential; Section J.1 explicitly states modifications had 'negligible effect' on Muon training
Overclaimed efficiency: all methods use same number of matrix-matrix products; advantage is not computational efficiency but polynomial choice quality

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis: Theorem 3.1 proves global optimality of the greedy polynomial composition approach using minimax approximation theory
Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates why existing matrix polar methods (QR, matrix inverses) are unsuitable for GPU-accelerated deep learning
Practical implementation with finite-precision considerations: Addresses real bfloat16 challenges and provides short, usable PyTorch code
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Tests on synthetic/real matrices, multiple data scales (1B and 10B tokens), extensive ablations, and cross-domain experiments
Thorough presentation and reproducibility: Complete proofs, implementations, hyperparameters, and honest ablation studies including failure cases
weaknesses: Limited novelty: The core idea (adaptive minimax polynomials) is from Zolo-pd (Nakatsukasa & Freund 2016) and Chen & Chow (2014); this extends it to general odd polynomials, which is incremental
Marginal empirical improvements: ~1.7% relative gain over Jordan's method on GPT-2-Large (3.340 vs 3.398); improvement shrinks to <1% with 10B tokens; no advantage on CIFAR or ViT experiments

Theory-practice disconnect: Figure 5 shows exact SVD achieves identical validation loss as 5-6 Polar Express iterations, suggesting approximation quality is not the bottleneck. Figure 9 shows Muon is insensitive to singular values below 10⁻³σ_max, undermining the minimax optimality premise

Ad-hoc implementation modifies the optimized problem: Safety factor (1.01), cushioning, and normalization fixes in Section 3.4 violate the theoretical optimization, raising questions about what is actually being solved
Dependence on unknown lower bound ℓ: Must be guessed; Figure 3 shows 2-order-of-magnitude errors significantly degrade performance, yet no principled selection strategy provided
Limited application scope: Highly specialized to polar decomposition; main application (Muon) is relatively new; no tests on models >774M parameters; Algorithm 3 shows no benefit in practice
Inconsistent experimental results: CIFAR experiments (Section H.3) show no advantage or worse performance; ViT results mixed; improvements only consistent on GPT-2 with carefully tuned learning rates
No statistical significance testing: Figures 1, 4, 6 lack error bars or confidence intervals; small improvements may be within noise

strengths: Strong theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.1 proves global optimality of the greedy polynomial composition strategy through elegant application of the Equioscillation Theorem
Rigorous convergence analysis (Theorem 3.3) showing super-exponential convergence with practical implications
Excellent practical engineering: careful treatment of finite-precision arithmetic (bfloat16), pre-computed offline coefficients, minimal dependencies
Consistent experimental improvements across multiple settings (1B and 10B token training, multiple learning rates) despite modest margins
Exceptional reproducibility: complete code implementations, detailed hyperparameters, proofs, and supplementary experiments
Comprehensive ablations and supplementary analysis (Section H) including discovery of Muon's insensitivity to small singular values
Clearly written with thorough literature review distinguishing contributions from prior work (Zolo-pd, Chen & Chow, Newton-Schulz)
weaknesses: Modest practical improvements in the target domain (~0.05-0.06 nats validation loss reduction) without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Limited generalization: no improvements on image classification (CIFAR-10/100, Figures 14-15) and only marginal gains on Vision Transformers (Figure 16), questioning broader applicability
Sensitivity to singular value bounds: Figure 3 shows significant performance degradation when ℓ is misspecified; the method is only 'robust' within limited ranges despite claims otherwise
Incremental novelty: core ideas derive from Zolo-pd (Nakatsukasa & Freund 2016) and Chen & Chow (2014); main novelty is the optimality proof, but concurrent work achieves similar adaptivity
Scope limited to Muon optimizer: practical impact depends on Muon adoption, which remains niche relative to Adam/AdamW in the broader ML community

Underdeveloped extensions: Spectrum-aware initialization (Section I) requires QR decomposition; Algorithm 3 for rectangular matrices (Section J) shows 'negligible effect' on actual runtime despite extensive development
Limited theoretical insight into why Muon converges with only 5-6 iterations despite Polar Express not fully converging; Section H.1 provides empirical rather than theoretical analysis
Potential selection bias in learning rate tuning: each method's 'best learning rate' is chosen independently, which could systematically favor one approach
